old: I developed several software tools to aid in the development of a human-mimetic robot driven by a neural model of control. To do this, I built the following five systems. 1) I adapted the Gait2392 human model in OpenSIM to an equivalent model in the physics simulator MuJoCo. I then connected it to the SNS-Toolbox and tested it with a CPG controller. 2) I developed a simulated BPA-routed robot counterpart to the Gait2392 Model, also coupled to a CPG controller. 3) I combined the Li walker and Deng neural model with foot-contact feedback and tested it... 4) I built a GUI for block-programming neural controllers that were attached mechanical models; 5) I coupled the SolidWorks robot assembly to MATLAB BPA models and a neural controller. These tools enable controlled comparisons of neural organization across biological and artificial actuation. I developed the specific converted models, actuator interfaces, graphical-library elements, and circuit implementations below to build and test those connections. The capability table identifies the connections demonstrated and those still incomplete.
new:
Researchers studying neuromechanical control need to distinguish movement generated by a neural circuit from movement shaped by sensory feedback, actuator mechanics, and external support. For the humanoid models studied here, the unresolved questions were whether a specified circuit retained its behavior when implemented in a different simulator, and how its output changed when coupled to human musculotendon mechanics or artificial muscles. A successful neural trace alone could not answer the mechanical question, and a moving model alone could not establish that the intended neural pathways caused the movement.

I addressed this gap by constructing models in which the neural pathways, actuator law, sensory inputs, and support conditions can be specified and varied, together with tests that distinguish circuit behavior from implementation and coupling errors. The resulting contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item A custom Li--Deng walker and controller, developed in AnimatLab and implemented in MuJoCo with SNS-Toolbox, with matched implementations of its contact-driven neural core in NumPy and Simulink.
    \item Gait2392-based neuromechanical models with alternative neural controllers, and a robot counterpart with BPA routing and the actuator-force model from Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles}.
    \item The SNS-Simscape block library and GUI for block programming neural pathways, including sensory, neuron, synapse, activation, and custom BPA-force blocks.
    \item A SolidWorks-derived robot assembly in Simscape Multibody coupled to a neural controller and BPA actuators using my force model.
    \item Integration of SNS-Simscape controllers with MuJoCo through the MathWorks bidirectional bridge, together with model-import procedures for musculoskeletal and CAD-derived mechanisms.
    \item A five-stage curriculum and experiment workflow for parameter searches, adjustable support, neural stimuli, pathway interventions, mechanical perturbations, and recording neural and mechanical outputs.
    \item Implementations of literature-derived circuits and selected spiking-neuron counterparts for comparing neural mechanisms and coding assumptions.
\end{enumerate}
Table~\ref{tab:sns_capability} gives selected functional-verification tests and proof-of-concept demonstrations. These establish that the tools can construct, exercise, and compare the specified models. The feedback experiments also provide a limited mechanistic result: removing particular sensory pathways can eliminate stepping in a fixed supported configuration, identifying a dependence that would not be apparent from its intact motion alone.
reason: Address advisor knowledge-gap request with concrete questions, contributions, and demonstrated answers; retain approved list order.

old: Existing software supplied separate parts of the solution. OpenSim supplied musculoskeletal geometry, MyoConverter translated it to MuJoCo, and SNS-Toolbox supplied neuron and synapse models \citep{delp_opensim_2007, caggiano_myosuite_2022, todorov_mujoco_2012, nourse_sns_2023}. The MuJoCo version used here supports scripted simulation and parameter searches but uses rigid tendons; its Python interface does not provide the block-based circuit assembly needed for this workflow. Simulink supplies that graphical construction, while Simscape Multibody imports mechanical geometry, including SolidWorks-derived mechanisms. AnimatLab retains the reference controllers but is unsupported, relies on an older physics engine, and ran these simulations slowly. The tools connect these complementary environments and use matched tests to check what transfers between them.

Simulink provided graphical block programming, and Simscape Multibody provided mechanical modeling and import of SolidWorks-derived mechanisms. My contributions are the particular model implementations, custom blocks, actuator integrations, and evaluation procedures built with those packages. The SNS-Simscape library makes the neural pathways explicit in a block diagram, while the MuJoCo implementations support repeated scripted evaluations and parameter searches. Matched-input tests check selected circuits before their outputs are interpreted as neural control of a mechanical model.

old: MyoConverter supplies the initial OpenSim-to-MuJoCo translation. I added repair and audit steps for the custom muscle paths and joint conventions, then coupled the converted model to an SNS-Toolbox controller. The converted model carries 92 muscle-tendon actuators. Geometry comparisons against the source and individual-actuator tests check that the conversion preserves the intended attachment paths and torque directions. The neural and mechanical models exchange signals at a \qty{2}{\milli\second} step.
new:
My first conversion attempt used the robot model, which combined BPA routing on the Gait2392 skeleton with unchanged human muscle parameters. MyoConverter's muscle-equilibrium checks rejected infeasible combinations of routed length and muscle parameters. I therefore separated conversion of the human reference from reconstruction of the robot routing. This distinction matters because an error caused by an artificial-actuator route should not be interpreted as a property of the original human model.

The human-model conversion also required specific repairs. Three small hip rotators per side, the quadratus femoris, gemelli, and piriformis, were disabled at model load. The converted model retains 92 actuator entries, but these six contribute no force. The model retains the OpenSim and International Society of Biomechanics coordinate convention; frame transformations and individual-actuator tests check that joint motion and torque directions have the intended signs.

The source represents patella motion through muscle insertion locations that vary with knee angle. In the converted model, limits on the joints representing these moving path points conflicted with their coupling constraints. Removing those conflicting limits allowed the coupled path points to follow their prescribed trajectories. The rectus femoris path also required a patella-tracking via point to restore its knee-extension action. Explicit collision pairs introduced unwanted contacts, so contact was restricted to the foot--ground pairs. The anatomical joint limits also had to be re-enabled; these driver joints were treated separately from the coupled path-point joints. Passive joint torques supplemented the joint behavior. These repairs explain why conversion needed checks beyond successful loading: a model could load while producing an incorrect torque direction or unintended contact force.

Comparisons with the OpenSim attachment paths and single-actuator tests checked the transferred geometry and force directions. They do not establish that every muscle reproduces the source force throughout its range or that the controller produces walking. The neural and mechanical models exchange signals at a \qty{2}{\milli\second} solver time step. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_conversion_repairs} records the individual repairs and their scope.
reason: Explain the actual conversion problems and repairs, including Ben's reply about the initial robotbody attempt.

old: The BPA interface evaluates the quasi-static actuator force model from Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles} using the simulated muscle length and pressure. It provides an actuator model for controller development, rather than a simulation of valve and pressure dynamics. The controller receives length, velocity, force, and contact signals through the corresponding sensory channels. The correction terms of Chapter~\ref{ch:torque} do not by themselves verify the transferred routing or compliance of a dynamic model; these require separate checks.
new: For artificial-muscle simulations, I implemented an actuator-force calculation that evaluates the quasi-static BPA model from Chapter~\ref{ch:muscles} at the current simulated actuator length and commanded pressure. The calculated tensile force acts along the model's specified tendon route. Length, velocity, force, and foot-contact measurements are then returned to the neural controller through sensory channels. This closes the neural-command--actuator-force--sensory-feedback loop. The calculation represents the measured static force dependence; it does not add valve-flow or pressure-transient dynamics. Routing geometry and dynamic force transmission therefore require their own checks beyond the isometric force fit.
reason: Define the BPA interface explicitly and connect it to the preceding conversion account.

old: The MuJoCo--Simulink bridge, built on the official MathWorks blockset that embeds the MuJoCo model inside Simulink as the mechanical model, was tested against an independent Python integration using single-muscle activation, different control rates, and sensor readback. Readback was bit-exact over the scored window. The exported neural network also drove all 92 actuators during a \qty{5}{\second} open-loop run, without afferent return; the closed-loop reflex experiment exercised commands and sensory measurements through the same interface. However, under tonic drive alone the Simulink realization reached a fixed point while the NumPy reference oscillated. The network-level discrepancy remains a limit on transferring tuned controller parameters between implementations.

old: The AnimatLab attempt motivated a repeatable way to connect neural circuits to mechanical models and test their individual interfaces. The resulting tools provide converted geometry, a BPA-force interface, graphical neural components, controller ports, and automated comparisons. The reflex and rhythm-core tests demonstrate specific circuit behaviors; the bridge tests demonstrate closed-loop signal exchange. Mechanical import, controller transfer, and locomotion performance remain separate validation problems.
new:
The principal contribution is a set of executable neuromechanical models and experimental tools that make the roles of neural pathways and actuator mechanics accessible to controlled tests. The initial AnimatLab model established the combined walker and CPG organization. The Gait2392 implementations extend controller development to a human-scale model with many joints and actuator channels, while the BPA implementations connect the measured actuator-force model to neural control. SNS-Simscape provides a graphical representation of the pathways, and the curriculum and experiment drivers provide repeatable changes in drive, support, feedback, and perturbation conditions.

The representative results answer different parts of the knowledge gap. Agreement between the NumPy and Simulink rhythm cores establishes that the specified circuit response can be preserved across those implementations under matched inputs. The loaded-arm comparison establishes a corrective effect of feedback in the coupled block model. The fixed-controller W2L ablation shows that its tested stepping behavior depends on contact and Ib-force feedback. The bridge tests establish the command and measurement exchange needed to carry out such experiments across software environments. Together, these results provide an operational method for separating implementation agreement, sensory contribution, and mechanical response.
reason: Connect each demonstrated result to the knowledge gap.

The supported demonstrations establish this experimental capability; they do not establish balance without the support rig or transfer of every controller between models. Chapter~\ref{ch:futurework} discusses extensions to weight-bearing control and hardware. Those extensions build on the models and tests already demonstrated here.

old: Attempts to implement neural control models exposes two further gaps. First, the project lacked a structured, searchable resource connecting measured sensory-afferent properties to the species, preparations, and pathway roles on which controller design depends. Those findings were distributed across primary papers and reviews \citep{van_de_crommert_review_1998, windhorst_muscle_2007, windhorst_spinal_2022}, and was difficult to sift through for new researchers to the field. Second, the project lacked validated neuromechanical models linking a spinal CPG to both a human-scale musculoskeletal model and its BPA-routed robot counterpart. Published CPG architectures and simulation tools supplied components \citep{rybak_modelling_2006, mccrea_organization_2008, markin_afferent_2010, nourse_sns_2023}, but they had not been combined into a complete into a complete human neuromechanical model that could be used for rigurous testing of different hypotheses. The SADb and simulation chapters address these evidence and implementation gaps, respectively.
new: Researchers implementing neural control models face two related problems. Sensory-afferent findings are distributed across species, preparations, and experimental protocols, so selecting a feedback pathway requires locating its measured properties and the conditions under which they were observed \citep{van_de_crommert_review_1998, windhorst_muscle_2007, windhorst_spinal_2022}. I addressed that evidence-access problem with the Sensory Afferent Database. A second problem arises when a published neural circuit is coupled to a different mechanical model: its behavior depends on the actuator mechanics, sensory signals, support conditions, and numerical implementation as well as on the circuit itself. Published architectures and software supply essential components \citep{rybak_modelling_2006, mccrea_organization_2008, markin_afferent_2010, nourse_sns_2023}, but the behavior of their particular combination must be established. I developed coupled human and artificial-muscle models, graphical neural blocks, and controlled evaluation procedures to distinguish these contributions. Representative tests establish circuit agreement across implementations, corrective reflex behavior, and the dependence of a supported stepping configuration on selected feedback pathways.
reason: Repair grammar and duplicated text; state evidence and neuromechanical knowledge gaps without claiming no prior human model exists.

old: \item \textbf{Develop tools and a framework for neuromechanical control} of the humanoid robot by converting its OpenSim musculoskeletal model to MuJoCo, implementing an SNS-Toolbox two-level spinal CPG with proprioceptive and heel/toe contact feedback, and establishing a staged tuning and verification workflow (Chapters~\ref{ch:sns} and~\ref{ch:overall}).
new: \item \textbf{Develop and demonstrate neuromechanical modeling tools} by implementing the Li--Deng walker, Gait2392-based models with alternative neural controllers and artificial-muscle actuation, SNS-Simscape blocks for neural pathways, and staged tuning and experiment procedures; verify representative circuit responses, implementation agreement, and neural--mechanical signal exchange (Chapters~\ref{ch:sns} and~\ref{ch:overall}).

old: The fourth enabler is the set of novel neuromechanical simulation tools (Chapter~\ref{ch:sns}): the audited OpenSim-to-MuJoCo conversion of the robot's musculoskeletal model, the force interface that computes actuator forces inside the loop from the validated BPA model, the two-level spinal networks built in SNS-Toolbox, the Simulink SNS library for assembly in a controls-engineering environment, the cross-engine verification harness, and the spiking-neuron mirrors that test the coding assumption. On these tools the controller program has matured from assembly into use. Supported stepping configurations have been tuned and evaluated in full-body simulations, the first pathway-deletion and drive-stimulus experiments have been run, the gait-validation sweep has measured how far the tuned networks remain from the diversity of human reference locomotion, and the contact-driven rhythm core has been shown to transfer between independent implementations with exact period agreement and trace correlations above 0.9999. In hardware, the companion balance-platform studies demonstrated that a BPA-actuated limb holds itself upright under pseudo-vestibular inertial feedback \citep{bolen_balance_2024, bolen_selfbalancing_2024, bolen_selfbalancing_srs_2024}. What remains unfinished is equally specific, and it organizes the future work below: the balance and weight-bearing layers that unsupported bilateral walking requires, wider transfer across reference cycles, the supraspinal sensorium, and embedded real-time execution.
new:
The fourth contribution is the set of neuromechanical modeling tools in Chapter~\ref{ch:sns}. The Li--Deng walker, Gait2392-based controller implementations, and BPA-force integrations provide defined combinations of neural and mechanical models. SNS-Simscape makes the neural pathways editable as block diagrams, and the experiment drivers vary support, neural drive, sensory pathways, and external perturbations. These tools address the difficulty of determining whether a change in movement arises from neural organization, actuator mechanics, or implementation differences. Matched rhythm-core tests establish agreement between selected NumPy and Simulink implementations; the loaded-arm demonstration shows corrective feedback; and the fixed-controller W2L ablation shows that the tested contact and force-feedback pathways sustain its supported stepping. The contribution is both the reusable experimental capability and these specific demonstrations of what it can distinguish.

The coupled-model results must be interpreted under their stated support conditions. Supported stepping and forward progression establish functioning neural--mechanical loops, while removal of tonic drive tests a different dependence from removal of mechanical support. The balance-platform studies provide a separate hardware demonstration of a BPA-actuated limb under pseudo-vestibular inertial feedback \citep{bolen_balance_2024, bolen_selfbalancing_2024, bolen_selfbalancing_srs_2024}. Together, the simulation tools and hardware precedents support further study of balance and weight bearing without treating those capabilities as already demonstrated by the stepping tests.
reason: Make the whole-work discussion reflect the completed SNS contributions and distinct evidence.

old: The tools also compose across programs, and the composition is now cheap enough to be a standard workflow. A full-body OpenSim model with arms and trunk, of the kind MyoSuite distributes \citep{caggiano_myosuite_2022}, can be brought into the SNS-Simscape library for graphical assembly and inspection of the controller, and the same network imported back into SNS-Toolbox on MuJoCo \citep{nourse_sns_2023} for the speed that tuning and long evaluations require. A controller built in that loop inherits the conversion audit, the cross-engine checks, and the deletion apparatus of Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} without rebuilding any of them.

Its controller could then be assembled or inspected with the neural block tools and evaluated with the relevant simulation interface. The matched-circuit tests and pathway-intervention procedures provide a reusable verification method, but each new model and controller combination must establish its own behavior.

old: The sensory-afferent resource of Chapter~\ref{ch:database} makes relevant physiological reports easier to locate and compare, while retaining the need to inspect their experimental context. Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} supplies tools for developing and checking neural models and mechanical interfaces. Independent implementations reproduced the contact-driven rhythm core with exact period agreement and trace correlations above 0.9999. Other checks exposed limitations, including a tonic operating-point mismatch in the MuJoCo bridge. Supported stepping and pathway experiments provide further development evidence, but no harness-free walking has been demonstrated in the program's records.
new: The Sensory Afferent Database in Chapter~\ref{ch:database} organizes physiological evidence by properties and experimental context, making it easier to select and assess candidate feedback pathways. Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} addresses the complementary problem of testing those pathways in coupled neural and mechanical models. I developed the Li--Deng walker implementations, Gait2392-based neuromechanical models, SNS-Simscape neural blocks and actuator integrations, and staged tuning and experiment procedures. Selected demonstrations establish implementation agreement for a contact-driven rhythm core, corrective feedback in a loaded-arm model, and feedback-dependent stepping in a fixed supported W2L configuration. These results show that the tools can distinguish circuit behavior, sensory contribution, and mechanical response under specified conditions.

The present findings concern the measured actuator and joint behavior and the specified simulation tests.

old: The dissertation provides experimentally grounded actuator and joint models, a curated afferent resource, and simulation tools for that work. Their scientific value lies in making assumptions explicit and testable as the project moves toward controlled neuromechanical experiments on a physical robot.
new: The dissertation provides experimentally grounded actuator and joint models, a curated afferent resource, and functioning neuromechanical modeling and evaluation tools. Together, they make actuator selection, torque prediction, sensory-pathway selection, and controlled simulation tests more explicit and reproducible. These are usable contributions to biomimetic robot design and to studying how neural control interacts with mechanical structure.
reason: Conclude with delivered scientific and methodological contributions.

old: The third line, in which this dissertation sits, is biologically grounded synthetic nervous systems: controllers whose neurons and synapses are explicit, conductance-based, and mapped to identified physiological circuits, simulated at speeds sufficient for real-time robotics \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Hierarchical CPG control is meanwhile spreading to bipedal-capable musculoskeletal models, including motor-module bipedal walkers \citep{ichimura_pathological_2019}, two-layer rhythm-generator and pattern-formation control of a musculoskeletal macaque model \citep{nishizaki_gait_2026}, and two-level CPG control of muscle-driven robotic hind legs \citep{fukuoka_autonomous_2021}, though always in simulation with generic musculature or on non-humanoid platforms; a two-layer SNS driving a custom-anatomy, artificial-muscle humanoid leg remains unclaimed. What distinguishes the present program from all three lines is the combination it attempts: an anatomically grounded controller (two-layer CPG with Ia, Ib, II, and contact feedback), a biomechanically validated pneumatic model (Chapter~\ref{ch:torque}), and an eventual physical robot.
new: The third line, in which this dissertation sits, uses synthetic nervous systems whose neurons and synapses explicitly represent candidate physiological circuits. SNS-Toolbox supports conductance-based networks at speeds suitable for selected real-time robotic applications \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Related work includes motor-module bipedal walkers \citep{ichimura_pathological_2019}, two-layer rhythm-generator and pattern-formation control of a musculoskeletal macaque model \citep{nishizaki_gait_2026}, and CPG control of muscle-driven robotic hind legs \citep{fukuoka_autonomous_2021}. These studies establish the value of coupled neural and mechanical models. For the humanoid design studied here, the remaining methodological question is how to implement and verify candidate spinal circuits with human musculotendon mechanics and custom BPA actuation, while distinguishing neural effects from conversion or coupling errors. Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} addresses that question through specific model implementations, graphical neural blocks, and controlled verification and feedback tests.
reason: Replace unsupported field-wide novelty claim with the scoped methodological gap; retain cited prior work.
